title: Boss: the fleet inventory
summary: Inventory a mixed fleet from its os-release files: one line per host, a count per family, and who is out of support.

steps.title: A mixed fleet
body: You inherited a mixed fleet: Ubuntu, Debian, Rocky, Alma, a forgotten CentOS, Alpine, SUSE, Amazon Linux and a few
desktops. An inventory job collected `/etc/os-release` and `uname -r` from each into `~/fleet`. Turn that into an
inventory, a count per family and a list of hosts that no longer get security updates.

steps.title: One line per machine
prompt: Your manager wants the fleet on one page. `~/fleet/HOST/` holds each host's `os-release` and `uname-r` (its kernel).
Write `~/answers/inventory.txt` with one line per host, sorted by host name, exactly like:
That is `HOST: PRETTY_NAME, kernel KERNEL`. These files came from other machines, so **parse** them (`sed`, `grep`, `cut`)

checks.name: inventory.txt has the right lines
checks.cmd: diff ~/answers/inventory.txt <(for d in ~/fleet/*/; do h=$(basename "$d"); p=$(sed -n 's/^PRETTY_NAME=//p' "$d/os-release" | tr -d '"'); echo "$h: $p, kernel $(cat "$d/uname-r")"; done)
checks.fail: The inventory does not match (diff below: `<` is yours, `>` is expected).

hints: Loop over the folders: `for d in ~/fleet/*/; do h=$(basename "$d"); ...; done > ~/answers/inventory.txt`. The glob is already sorted.
`sed -n 's/^PRETTY_NAME=//p' "$d/os-release" | tr -d '"'` gives the name without quotes.
solution: for d in ~/fleet/*/; do h=$(basename "$d"); p=$(sed -n 's/^PRETTY_NAME=//p' "$d/os-release" | tr -d '"'); echo "$h: $p, kernel $(cat "$d/uname-r")"; done > ~/answers/inventory.txt
steps.explain: On a real fleet the collection step is `ssh host cat /etc/os-release` in a loop, or Ansible facts (`ansible all -m setup -a filter=ansible_distribution*`). The parsing is the same. Look at the kernels too: a 3.10 kernel on CentOS 7 tells you before any table does that the box is ancient.

steps.title: Count the fleet by family
prompt: `~/bin/osfamily FILE` (it works now) names a host's family. Write into `~/answers/families.txt` how many hosts each
family has, as `count family` lines, biggest first, ties by family name, exactly what

checks.name: families.txt counts the families
checks.fail: The counts do not match (diff below). Run `osfamily` on each host's file, then count the lines.

hints: `for f in ~/fleet/*/os-release; do ~/bin/osfamily "$f"; done` prints one family per host.
Pipe that into `sort | uniq -c`: `uniq` only merges **adjacent** lines, so sort first.
`... | sort | uniq -c | sort -k1,1nr -k2 > ~/answers/families.txt`: by count descending, then by name.
solution: for f in ~/fleet/*/os-release; do ~/bin/osfamily "$f"; done | sort | uniq -c | sort -k1,1nr -k2 > ~/answers/families.txt
steps.explain: Counting by family tells you how many runbooks, base images and patch pipelines you really maintain. A fleet with six families is six times the work of a fleet with one, which is the usual argument for standardising.

steps.title: Which hosts are out of support?
prompt: `~/fleet/support.csv` lists when each release stops getting free security updates (`id,version,ends`). A row matches a
host when its `ID` equals `id` and its `VERSION_ID` **is** `version` or **starts with** `version.` (Rocky `9.6` is
Write `~/answers/past-eol.txt`: every host whose support **ended before 2026-11-26**, as `HOST ID VERSION_ID ENDS`,
sorted by host. Hosts with no matching row (like the rolling one) are left out. Dates in `YYYY-MM-DD` form compare
correctly as plain strings, so `awk` can compare them with `<`.

checks.name: past-eol.txt lists the right hosts
checks.fail: The report does not match (diff below: `<` is yours, `>` is expected). Check the version rule: `9.6` matches the row `9`.

hints: Per host, get `ID` and `VERSION_ID` (`sed -n 's/^ID=//p'` and strip quotes), then look them up in the CSV with `awk -F,`.
In awk: `$1 == id && (v == $2 || index(v, $2 ".") == 1) && $3 < "2026-11-26"`. Pass shell values in with `-v id="$id" -v v="$v"`.

One way: `for d in ~/fleet/*/; do h=$(basename "$d"); id=$(sed -n 's/^ID=//p' "$d/os-release" | tr -d '"'); v=$(sed -n 's/^VERSION_ID=//p' "$d/os-release" | tr -d '"'); awk -F, -v h="$h" -v id="$id" -v v="$v" 'NR>1 && $1==id && (v==$2 || index(v,$2".")==1) && $3<"2026-11-26" {print h, id, v, $3}' ~/fleet/support.csv; done > ~/answers/past-eol.txt`.
solution: for d in ~/fleet/*/; do h=$(basename "$d"); id=$(sed -n 's/^ID=//p' "$d/os-release" | tr -d '"'); v=$(sed -n 's/^VERSION_ID=//p' "$d/os-release" | tr -d '"'); awk -F, -v h="$h" -v id="$id" -v v="$v" 'NR>1 && $1==id && (v==$2 || index(v,$2".")==1) && $3<"2026-11-26" {print h, id, v, $3}' ~/fleet/support.csv; done > ~/answers/past-eol.txt
explain: Five hosts with no security updates is a finding for the next audit. The fixes differ: an interim Ubuntu moves to the
next LTS, Debian 11 to 13 (one major at a time: 11 to 12 to 13), CentOS 7 needs a migration to Rocky or AlmaLinux (or paid
extended support), and openSUSE Leap 15.6 moves to 16.0. Keep the support table in the repo next to the inventory script
and check the vendors' lifecycle pages when you update it.
